source: Thakkar et al. (2025) Can LLM feedback enhance review quality? Randomized study of 20K reviews at ICLR 2025
finding: Corrects claim K19/c11. Reviews were randomised to get LLM feedback or not. About 26.6% of feedback recipients updated the review, against 9.4% of controls. Feedback came from a multi-call agent plus LLM reliability tests that blocked bad feedback.
numbers: 44,831 reviews on 11,553 papers. About 50% selected for feedback; 18,946 (42.3%) actually received it (7.9% of selected got none, mostly because the agent judged feedback unneeded). 5,031 updated (26.6%); control 2,103 of 22,364 updated (9.4%), a gap of about 17 points. Mean length change: control +7.0 words, feedback group +21.0 (p<0.01); updated reviews +80.3 vs +2.1 words for not updated. 12,222 feedback items incorporated; 89% of updaters used at least one item; 17.7% of all items were incorporated. More than 96% of generated feedback passed all reliability tests.
limits: Reviewers knew the feedback was LLM-made. Score edits barely differed (8.1% vs 7.5%, p<0.05) and mean score change did not differ. No ground truth for decision accuracy. Effect measured is engagement and length, not correctness.
agent_relevance: A structured second-pass critique with guardrail tests changes behaviour at scale; it is an institution-style check.

source: Thakkar et al. (2025), blinded quality annotation and rebuttal engagement
finding: The human quality check was small: two annotators, 100 review pairs. They preferred the updated review in 89% of pairs. Feedback recipients also engaged more in rebuttal and edited scores slightly more often.
numbers: 89% preference on 100 pairs; 8.1% vs 7.5% of reviewers edited any score (p<0.05); no significant difference in mean score change (Appendix C).
quote: Human annotators preferred modified reviews 89% of the time (out of 100 examples)
limits: N=2 annotators, N=100; no inter-rater statistic seen in the text read. The earlier claim '27% of 20,000+ reviewers' conflated 26.6% of 18,946 recipients with the 20K headline.
agent_relevance: Do not cite the 27% as an accuracy gain. Cite it as evidence that a structured critique changes what reviewers write.

source: Schmidgall and Moor (2025) AgentRxiv, full text
finding: Full text read. Agent labs with access to earlier reports kept improving on MATH-500; labs without access plateaued. The tracked number is the highest test accuracy seen so far, not a held-out score.
numbers: Base gpt-4o-mini 70.2%. With access to prior papers: best 78.2% (paper states +11.4%; that is 8.0 points). Without access (isolated): plateau at 73.4% and 73.8% after about 10 papers. Best method SDA transfers: MMLU-Pro 63.1 to 70.8, MedQA 74.9 up, mean +3.3% across benchmarks and models. Per-paper cost about $3.11 (max $9.87), 1.36 hours average.
quote: agents with access to their prior research achieve higher performance improvements compared to agents operating in isolation
limits: Accuracy tracked is the best MATH-500 test accuracy across papers, so selection happens on the test set. Only two isolated curves. Authors report reward hacking and hallucination in paper writing.
agent_relevance: Memory of earlier attempts helps in a narrow loop, but part of the gain is search on the test set. Use a held-out split before trusting it.

source: Schmidgall and Moor (2025) AgentRxiv, parallel labs and cost
finding: Three labs sharing one server reached 79.8% at best and 78.7% on average, versus 77.4% for three extra sequential runs. The parallel setup used three times the compute, so it is not an equal-token comparison.
numbers: Three labs x 40 papers = 120 papers vs 40 sequential. Cost +$187.6 (+203.9%) over the $92.0 sequential run. 76.2% reached after 7 papers in parallel vs 23 papers sequential. Best 79.8% vs 78.2% (+2.0 points); mean 78.7% vs 78.2% (+0.7); +3.4 vs the three-run sequential mean of 77.4%.
limits: MATH-500 plus transfer tests only; gpt-4o-mini in the loop; authors note redundant overlapping ideas.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open: no clean equal-token test of shared memory vs isolated runs, and no replication beyond MATH-500.

source: Sakana AI (2025) The AI Scientist-v2, full text
finding: Re-read. One of three fully AI-written papers got workshop scores 6, 6, 7 (mean 6.33, top 45% of 43 submissions). Papers were chosen from several seeds and a human-selected idea pool, and the authors' own review said none met main-track standards.
numbers: 3 manuscripts among 43 ICBINB (ICLR 2025 workshop) submissions; the accepted one was withdrawn. Multiple manuscripts per idea with different seeds; the best-looking one per idea was submitted. Authors report citation errors and hallucination.
limits: 1 success of 3, workshop not main track, reviewers told some papers might be AI-made. Selection of submitted papers is a free degree of freedom. No independent replication found in this session (web search budget exhausted).
agent_relevance: Do not use it as an acceptance rate.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: With an automatic verifier (unit tests, proof checker), more samples turn straight into more solved problems. Without one, majority voting and reward models plateau while coverage keeps rising.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 (single-sample SOTA 43%). CodeContests, Gemma-2B: 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000 samples. MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority vote or reward-model selection moves only 40.50% to 41.41%; they plateau near 100 samples.
quote: verifiers must be able to find the needle in the haystack
limits: Compared by number of samples, not matched total tokens against a judge pass. Verifier-gap result is for math word problems with one reward model.
agent_relevance: Support for gap 1: an executed check turns extra candidates into accuracy; a vote or judge does not. Still no matched-token run on our agent.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate
finding: Five debate methods on 9 benchmarks and 4 models mostly fail to beat Chain-of-Thought or Self-Consistency, even with much more compute. More agents or rounds usually do not help. The one clear winner (AgentVerse on HumanEval) adds an execution step.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini: SoM below CoT on all 9 datasets; ChatEval and AgentVerse beat CoT on only 1 of 9. Claude-3.5-haiku MMLU: only AgentVerse above CoT (+0.85%); others -3.60% or worse. Rounds 2 to 4 and agents 3 to 9: stagnation or decline in most cases. Heter-MAD (two model families, p=0.5 each): Heter-SoM +6.4% over SoM-average, Heter-EoT +8.2%; up to +5.8% over CoT-average.
quote: MAD often fail to outperform simple single-agent baselines
limits: Accuracy only; diversity of answers not measured. Fixed protocols with majority vote.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: debate does not beat independent samples plus vote; model heterogeneity helps; execution beats discussion.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD?
finding: Debate protocols do not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling. They are sensitive to hyperparameters; tuning the agent agreement level can lift one above all non-debate protocols.
numbers: Protocols compared by API calls (2.5 to 15) and accuracy: Society of Mind, Multi-Persona, ChatEval, Ensemble Refinement, Medprompt, self-consistency, single agent.
limits: Only abstract, method text and figure labels read; the numeric table was not extracted.
agent_relevance: An agreement-intensity knob controls conformity. Independent first answers, compared only afterwards, is the safer default.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: Across 70+ models, answers to open-ended prompts are alike within one model and across models. Ensembling different models gives little spread. LLM judges and reward models track humans less well when answers are of similar quality.
numbers: INFINITY-CHAT: 26K real queries; 31,250 human annotations, 25 raters per item. 25 models x 50 samples at top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0: average within-prompt pairwise similarity usually above 0.8; across 42 models 0.821. At min-p with temperature 2.0 still above 0.8. Between models 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82; vs gpt-4o 0.81). Correlation with human ratings drops on similar-quality subsets for LMs, reward models and 4 LM judges.
quote: different models produce strikingly similar outputs
limits: Embedding similarity on open-ended chat prompts, not novelty of scientific ideas.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 second half: more samples from one family add little spread, so a larger ensemble is not a route to novelty. Use different models or forced distinct frames.

source: Verga et al. (2024) Replacing judges with juries (PoLL)
finding: A panel of three smaller judges from different families agrees with humans more than one GPT-4 judge, and costs about seven times less.
numbers: Cohen's kappa vs humans on NQ/TQA/HPQA: GPT-4 0.627/0.841/0.830; Haiku 0.749/0.894/0.873; PoLL 0.763/0.906/0.867. Panel is seven to eight times cheaper than GPT-4.
limits: Three judge settings, six datasets, one panel size (three). No curve of agreement against number of judges.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partial: three diverse judges beat one big one. No curve to a 70% agreement target.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Judging LLM-as-a-judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
finding: GPT-4 agrees with humans over 80%, the same as human-human agreement, but judges show position bias, verbosity bias and weak maths grading.
numbers: Position consistency after swapping answer order: GPT-4 65.0% (default) and 66.2% (renamed prompt), GPT-3.5 46.2%, Claude-v1 23.8% (75.0% favour first). Few-shot lifts GPT-4 consistency from 65.0% to 77.5%. Self-enhancement: GPT-4 +10% win rate for itself, Claude-v1 +25%; authors say data are too small to conclude.
quote: Only GPT-4 outputs consistent results in more than 60% of cases.
limits: 2023 models. Prestige or affiliation bias not tested. Pataranutaporn 2025 could not be located (arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs rate-limited, search budget spent).
agent_relevance: Gap 8: swap order and score twice as a cheap blind. Prestige bias in our own judge is untested.

source: Wu, Wang and Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt, full text
finding: Re-opened. Disruption falls with team size across papers, patents and software; about two thirds of the effect is within the same scientists.
numbers: More than 50 million teams, 1954-2014. Disruption drops 70% (papers), 30% (patents), 50% (software) from 1 to 50 members. Solo authors 72% more likely than 5-person teams to be in top 5% disruption; 10-person teams 50% more likely to score a hit by citations. 86% of journals have a negative slope (91% of those with over 3,000 articles; 88% significant). Author-fixed-effects beta -0.00018 vs random effects -0.00027 (both p<0.001). One third of the effect appears only across different scientists.
limits: Observational. Engineering and computer science are exceptions because conference papers are not in the data. The disruption index has known flaws (b19).
agent_relevance: Team size is confounded with kind of problem. Do not read ensemble size as a causal handle on novelty.

source: Park, Leahey and Funk (2023) Papers and patents are becoming less disruptive over time, Nature 613:138-144
finding: Abstract read via Europe PMC only. 45 million papers and 3.9 million patents, six datasets, CD index. Decline holds across fields and several metrics, and is linked to narrower use of prior knowledge.
numbers: 45 million papers, 3.9 million patents, six decades; 198 citations in Europe PMC.
limits: Full text not opened (page redirected to login). Figures beyond the abstract rest on b17. Holst critique still second-hand (b18).

source: Boyle (1660) New Experiments Physico-Mechanicall, OCR of first edition
finding: Primary text read through rough OCR. Boyle admits his pump leaks, says it is useful to recite failed experiments, and cites repeats before named witnesses.
numbers: Mercury in the tube usually stood at about 29 and a half inches. After the first stroke it fell 18.5 and 19.5 inches in a small vessel in two tries. One experiment repeated 'in the presence of' Dr Wallis, Dr Ward and Mr Wren. Failure text: 'it is usefull to recite what Experiments miscarry as well as what succeed'. Leak text: 'our Receiver leak'd too fast' for a heat test.
quote: it is usefull to recite what Experiments miscarry as well as what succeed
limits: OCR is rough (long s); quotes lightly normalised. One book; not the Hobbes or Huygens exchange.
agent_relevance: This is the practice Shapin and Schaffer analyse: log failures, instrument defects and named witnesses. It supports G2.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Robert Boyle
finding: Boyle himself held that failed or once-only experiments should still be reported, and that the same procedure, materials and experimenters could give different outcomes. More witnesses raise probability.
numbers: Quoted: many experiments 'do not succeed, while others do succeed once but are then unable to be replicated' (section 2.2.3). Certain Physiological Essays 1661. Shapin and Schaffer and Huygens are not mentioned on the page.
limits: Encyclopedia summary, secondary. First 100,000 of 117,820 characters read. Does not cover the pump replication affair.
agent_relevance: Replication trouble was known to Boyle; the dispute was about what to do with it.

source: Franklin and Perovic, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Experiment in Physics (on Collins)
finding: Collins: a good apparatus is one that gives correct results, so no independent test exists and the regress ends by negotiation in the community. Franklin disputes this.
numbers: Weber gravity-wave case: six negative experiments; critics shared data and analysis programs, injected pulses of known energy and tested longer pulses, while Weber's group 'could not detect such calibration pulses'; one programming error produced spurious coincidences. Franklin: 'the critics' results were far more credible than Weber's'.
limits: First 100,000 of 157,913 characters read; TEA laser case not in what was read. Secondary source, not Collins' book.
agent_relevance: K03 stays contested. The way out in the Weber case was independent calibration, the schema's O-test.

source: Gap 1 status check from logged and new sources
finding: Evidence for gap 1 is indirect. Judged ideas fall after execution (Si et al., N=43); verifier selection beats voting at scale (d06); the execution step is what lifted AgentVerse (d07). No run on our agent.
numbers: Gaps -1.049 novelty, -1.760 excitement, -1.879 effectiveness (b12); 15.9% to 56% with a verifier, 40.50% to 41.41% for voting (d06).
limits: Three different task types; none matched on total tokens against a judge pass.
agent_relevance: Use an executed test as the default selector where one exists. The matched-token experiment on our agent is still needed.
